caustica.options.rt.title: Ray Tracing Settings
caustica.options.sharc.title: SHaRC Settings
caustica.options.sharc.enabled.tooltip: Enable NVIDIA's Spatial Hash Radiance Cache (SHaRC) experimental path-tracing cache. Every shaded surface warms a world-space voxel cache with its outgoing light and pushes that light back into the voxels of earlier path bounces; from the start bounce on, diffuse surfaces read the cache instead of tracing another noisy continuation, which shortens path tails, reduces multi-bounce noise and improves performance once warm. Works on any Vulkan ray-tracing GPU Caustica already supports.
caustica.options.sharc.cellSize.tooltip: Edge length of each SHaRC cache voxel, in blocks. Smaller cells are more accurate but warm up more slowly and thrash more; larger cells converge faster but blur light across larger regions.
caustica.options.sharc.cacheEntries.tool: Number of entries in the flat spatial-hash cache. Larger caches cover more world before entries collide and writes get rejected; smaller caches use less GPU memory but thrash sooner. NVIDIA recommends very large power-of-two capacities.
caustica.options.sharc.updateCoverage.to: Fraction of shaded paths that actually write to the cache. Higher refreshes the voxel cache faster but costs more bandwidth and temporally changes the cache more often.
caustica.options.sharc.temporalBlend.too: Inverse length of the temporal averaging window: the cache keeps roughly 1/value frames of history (12% blends over ~8 frames). Low values are smoother and slower to react; high values track lighting changes faster but flicker.
caustica.options.sharc.startBounce.toolt: First path bounce allowed to query the SHaRC cache. Earlier bounces keep tracing and only warm the cache. Higher values leave more bounces fully traced (more accurate but noisier); lower values engage the cache sooner (quieter but more approximate).
caustica.options.sharc.strength.tooltip: Scale applied to the cached radiance that replaces a vertex's shading and the rest of its path. 100% is NVIDIA's behaviour (full replacement); lower values darken the cached GI tail in exchange for softer cache transitions.
caustica.options.sharc.frameLifetime.too: How many frames a cache entry stays usable before it is treated as stale. Longer lifetimes converge more, but can keep old light around after large lighting changes.
caustica.options.sharc.normalThreshold.t: Minimum agreement (cosine) between the stored surface normal and the query normal for a cache hit. Lower allows hits on differently-oriented surfaces (more reuse, more bias); higher restricts hits to similarly-oriented surfaces.
caustica.options.sharc.stableFrames.tool: Minimum number of accumulated samples a cache entry needs before the tracer may use it. A single sample is already as good as the path it replaces, so 1 is the default; raise it if brand-new cells pop in as a flash when the camera moves.
caustica.options.sharc.debug.tooltip: Print a periodic SHaRC summary (cell size, entries, update coverage, blend, start bounce, strength, lifetime, normal threshold, min samples) to the console while SHaRC is active. State transitions and cache resets are always logged. Debug view 13 (Ray Tracing Settings > Debug View) paints per-pixel cache query results: green = hit, red = miss, grey = not queried.
caustica.options.sharc.reset.tooltip: Discard every cached SHaRC entry so the cache re-converges from scratch. Useful after moving a long distance or when a lighting change looks stale.
caustica.options.rt.exposureMode.tooltip: How the ray-traced image is mapped to display brightness. Auto adapts to scene luminance; Manual uses the exposure value directly.
caustica.options.rt.manualEv.tooltip: Exposure compensation in stops. In Manual, this is the fixed exposure. In Auto, this biases the auto exposure brighter or darker.
caustica.options.rt.spp.tooltip: Path-tracing samples taken per pixel each frame. Higher is cleaner but more demanding.
caustica.options.rt.maxBounces.tooltip: Maximum number of secondary path-tracing bounces after the primary hit. Higher captures more indirect light but costs more.
caustica.options.rt.sunSize.tooltip: Angular radius of the sun and moon disk. Larger discs cast softer shadow penumbrae.
caustica.options.rt.entities.tooltip: Include entities and block entities in the ray-traced scene.
caustica.options.rt.particles.tooltip: Draw particles as camera-ray billboards inside the traced scene.
caustica.options.rt.weatherParticles.too: Draw rain and snow as real geometry inside the traced scene. The columns come from Minecraft's own weather system, so they stop correctly at the ground, at leaves and under roofs, and fall as usual. Requires Ray-Traced Particles.
caustica.options.rt.omm.tooltip: Speeds up grass, leaves and other cutout blocks by skipping the any-hit test on provably opaque regions. If you ever see visual corruption or crashes around cutout terrain (rare, driver-dependent), turn this off — the terrain rebuilds without them. Note: if they were disabled at game launch, the Vulkan feature only engages after re-entering a world.
caustica.options.rt.rainDensity.tooltip: How thick ray-traced rain and snow appear. 100% is the full vanilla downpour; lower values thin the streaks into a light drizzle. 0% hides precipitation entirely while the overcast sky and dimming still follow the weather.
caustica.options.rt.glow.tooltip: Draw the vanilla Glowing-effect outline (through walls) around glowing entities.
caustica.options.rt.waterWaves.tooltip: Displace the water surface into real animated waves instead of scrolling a repeating texture. Crests and troughs move, and so do their highlights and caustics.
caustica.options.rt.waterOpacity.tooltip: How much light passes through water. Raise this if DLSS Ray Reconstruction draws a halo around water in dark places.
caustica.options.rt.sss.tooltip: Let light scatter through thin surfaces such as leaves and grass, so foliage glows when you look through it toward the sun. Only affects materials that provide subsurface data; costs an extra shadow ray where it applies.
caustica.options.rt.weatherLighting.tool: Dim sunlight and moonlight and darken the sky during rain and thunderstorms, and hide the sun, moon and stars behind the clouds. Off keeps clear-sky lighting in all weather.
caustica.options.rt.clouds.tooltip: Draw a cloud deck in the ray-traced sky. Caustica replaces the vanilla world renderer, which is where vanilla's own clouds are drawn, so this is what puts clouds back in the sky. The deck is visible in reflections and can shadow the world below.
caustica.options.rt.cloudStyle.tooltip: How clouds are drawn. Classic reproduces Minecraft's flat, blocky cloud layer. Volumetric ray-marches the clouds as real 3D shapes with depth, self-shadowing and light scattering, like heavy shaderpacks - much better looking, but noticeably more demanding. Both use the same cloud shapes, so switching does not move the clouds.
caustica.options.rt.skyStyle.tooltip: Choose between the improved vivid pastel sky and the original vanilla-like sky.
caustica.options.rt.cloudHeight.tooltip: World height the bottom of the clouds sits at. Vanilla's clouds sit at Y 192; the default here is higher because these clouds have real thickness, which makes a low deck feel much closer than vanilla's flat sheet. Raise it if the clouds feel too close to the ground. Measures the cloud base, so changing thickness does not move it.
caustica.options.rt.cloudThickness.toolt: How tall the clouds are. 0% makes them a flat sheet; higher values give them real 3D depth you can fly into. Classic clouds become solid boxes with bright tops and darker sides like vanilla's, and volumetric clouds become tall, billowing cumulus. This changes their shape only, not how see-through they are - use Cloud Opacity for that. Thicker clouds cost more performance.
How much the cloud deck dims the sunlight and moonlight reaching the ground under it. 0% draws clouds that cast no shadow at all; 100% lets a solid cloud block the sun completely. Costs no extra rays.
caustica.options.rt.cloudOpacity.tooltip: How solid the clouds are. 0% is fully transparent (clouds are skipped entirely); 100% is as solid as the cloud shape gets. This is a hard ceiling: at 20% a cloud is never more than 20% opaque, no matter how thick it is or how far away it is, so it never fills in toward the horizon.
caustica.options.rt.denoiser.tooltip: Apply the DLSS Ray Reconstruction denoising filter to the path-traced image. Off shows the raw, noisy trace at full resolution — useful as a reference view, but far grainier at low sample counts. Requires DLSS Ray Reconstruction support.
caustica.options.rt.handFov.tooltip: Make the first-person hand and held item follow the game's FOV setting. On, a higher FOV pushes the arm further away and a lower FOV brings it closer. Off restores vanilla's fixed hand FOV.
caustica.options.rt.hdr.tooltip: Present in HDR (ST.2084/PQ) instead of SDR, when the display supports it. Takes effect after restarting the game.
caustica.options.rt.hdrPaperWhite.toolti: Absolute brightness (in nits) that SDR-equivalent scene brightness maps to on an HDR display.
caustica.options.rt.hdrPeak.tooltip: Absolute brightness (in nits) highlights roll off toward. Set to your display's peak HDR brightness.
caustica.options.rt.dlssQuality.tooltip: DLSS Ray Reconstruction quality mode. Lower-quality modes render fewer pixels and upscale more aggressively for higher framerates; higher-quality modes render more pixels for a sharper image. Only affects the image when DLSS Ray Reconstruction is enabled.
caustica.options.rt.dlssPreset.tooltip: Selects the DLSS Ray Reconstruction neural model. DLSS 3.7 uses the official stable model; DLSS 4.5 enables the new experimental transformer model (Preset F).
caustica.options.rt.upscaler.tooltip: How the ray-traced image reaches display resolution. Off traces at native resolution with no upscaling. DLSS uses NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction, which denoises and upscales in a single pass (requires a supported GPU). FSR 3 is AMD FidelityFX Super Resolution: experimental and upscales without denoising. XeSS is Intel XeSS Super Resolution: an experimental ML upscaler (a trained neural network over the trace, motion vectors and depth) and is bundled for Windows only.
caustica.options.rt.fsrQuality.tooltip: AMD FSR 3 upscaler quality mode. Lower-quality modes render fewer pixels and upscale more aggressively for higher framerates; higher-quality modes render more pixels for a sharper image.
caustica.options.rt.xessQuality.tooltip: Intel XeSS upscaler quality mode. Lower-quality modes render fewer pixels and upscale more aggressively for higher framerates; higher-quality modes render more pixels for a sharper image.
caustica.options.rt.denoise.tooltip: The renderer's own denoiser (SVGF): reprojects the previous frames using the tracer's motion vectors, validating each pixel against last frame's depth and normals, then filters with a variance-guided wavelet cascade. Removes the 1 SPP noise while keeping detail crisp, and stays stable while the camera moves. Turn it off only to inspect the raw path-traced image.
caustica.options.rt.nrd.tooltip: NVIDIA Real-time Denoisers (REBLUR): denoises diffuse and specular separately from demodulated per-lobe radiance, with hit-distance driven kernels plus NVIDIA's anti-lag, anti-firefly and temporal stabilization. Usually cleaner on reflections than the built-in denoiser and costs more GPU. Replaces the built-in denoiser while it is on; pair it with FSR 3 / XeSS or no upscaler.
caustica.options.rt.nrdValidation.toolti: REBLUR's diagnostic overlay (debug): replaces the image with NRD's 16-viewport grid — inputs, per-pixel accumulated frame counts, disocclusion/occlusion state. For debugging temporal artifacts; set the upscaler to Off for a crisp readout.
caustica.options.rt.frameGeneration.tool: DLSS Frame Generation synthesizes intermediate frames to multiply the perceived frame rate. EXPERIMENTAL: may increase latency or cause artifacts. Requires the DLSS upscaler and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 40 or 50 series GPU.
caustica.options.rt.frameGeneration.unsu: Unavailable on this GPU: DLSS Frame Generation requires an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 40 or 50 series card. Support comes from the driver's NGX capability query once active, and from the GPU name otherwise.
Frame Generation via Caustica's own engine (Experimental): synthesizes intermediate frames between the actually rendered frames using the path tracer's exact motion vectors, multiplying the perceived frame rate on your display (2x–4x via the multiplier selector). Works on any GPU, at the cost of extra GPU work and a little added latency. If the native engine is switched off in the config, frame generation falls back to AMD FSR 3.1 (limited to 2x there).
caustica.options.rt.fgMultiplier.tooltip: How many frames your display receives per rendered frame. Higher = smoother motion at the cost of more GPU work and latency. Caustica's native frame generation engine interpolates with the tracer's own motion vectors and supports up to 4x; the AMD FSR 3.1 fallback engine (config 'native-engine' off) is fixed at 2x, since its runtime generates exactly one interpolated frame per rendered frame.
caustica.options.rt.debugView.tooltip: Visualize an intermediate ray-tracing buffer instead of the final image.
caustica.options.rt.blockEmissiveIntensi: Scales light emitted by blocks placed in the world, including torches, glowstone, lanterns, lava and other emissive surfaces.
caustica.options.rt.dynamicIntensity.too: Scales light emitted by luminous items held in hand, such as torches, lanterns and lava buckets, and by other dynamic emitters. Higher values brighten the area around you.
caustica.options.rt.heldItemLight.toolti: Cast a dynamic light from luminous items held in hand, such as torches, lanterns and lava buckets. Each item lights the world in its own colour. Turn off to stop held items lighting the world.
caustica.options.rt.restirSampling.toolt: Reuses validated light samples from previous frames and nearby pixels to reduce direct and indirect lighting noise. Turning this off uses the original independent ray-sampling method and releases the ReSTIR history buffers.
caustica.options.rt.tonemapOperator.tool: Selects the HDR-to-SDR tonemapping curve used after exposure.
caustica.options.rt.tonemapExposure.tool: Extra exposure bias, in EV stops, applied in the tonemapping pass after the auto/manual exposure value.
caustica.options.rt.tonemapGamma.tooltip: Final gamma/look adjustment applied after the selected tonemap curve. 1.00 leaves the curve unchanged.
caustica.options.rt.tonemapSaturation.to: Final saturation multiplier applied after tonemapping. 1.00 is neutral; 0.00 is grayscale.
caustica.options.rt.tonemapContrast.tool: Final contrast multiplier around middle gray applied after tonemapping. 1.00 is neutral.
caustica.options.rt.parallax.tooltip: Enable shader-only Parallax Occlusion Mapping from the LabPBR _n alpha channel. Geometry and BLASes are never rebuilt.
caustica.options.rt.parallaxStrength.too: Virtual POM relief depth. This creates no extra triangles.
caustica.options.rt.parallaxSmoothing.to: Switch LabPBR normal and surface sampling between smooth bilinear and crisp pixel-aligned sampling. POM relief stays pixel-exact either way: it intersects the height map as per-texel columns.
caustica.options.rt.parallaxDistance.too: Distance in blocks at which parallax smoothly disappears. Relief stays full through 80% of the selected range.
caustica.options.voxy.enabled.tooltip: Enable Voxy distant terrain in the Caustica path tracer. This takes effect immediately.
caustica.options.voxy.ingest.tooltip: Allow Voxy to ingest and save newly loaded Minecraft chunks. Existing cached LODs remain available when disabled.
caustica.options.voxy.distance.tooltip: Maximum horizontal distance of Voxy terrain. Increasing it uses more memory and takes longer to populate.
caustica.options.rt.frameGeneration.nati: Frame Generation via Caustica's own engine: this GPU doesn't have DLSS Frame Generation (RTX 40/50 series only), so Caustica's native motion-vector interpolation engine takes over — same toggle, multiplier up to 4x. Costs a little extra GPU work and latency.
caustica.options.rt.reflex.tooltip: NVIDIA Reflex low-latency mode: the driver paces frame submission so frames finish just in time for the display — less delay between your input and the screen. Pairs especially well with Frame Generation (FG costs about one rendered frame of latency; Reflex removes the rest of the pipeline queue). May slightly reduce maximum FPS — that's the latency/throughput trade.
caustica.options.rt.reflex.unsupported.t: Unavailable: the VK_NV_low_latency2 extension was not enabled on this device (requires a recent NVIDIA driver).
caustica.options.rt.metallicShininess.to: Polishes surfaces authored as metallic by reducing their roughness. 0% keeps the resource pack's material response; higher values make metallic reflections sharper without changing non-metal blocks or bloom.
caustica.options.rt.resetToDefaults.tool: Restore every setting on this page to its factory default. Only this page is affected; other pages and the startup-only options keep their values.
caustica.options.rt.resetAll: Reset All RT Settings to Defaults
caustica.options.rt.resetAll.tooltip: Restore EVERY Caustica setting exposed in these menus to its factory default in one click. Options that only apply at startup (config file or -Dcaustica.* flags) are untouched.
caustica.options.rt.moonSize.tooltip: Angular radius of the moon disc. Larger discs cast softer shadow penumbrae from moonlight. The night-time twin of the Sun Size slider.
caustica.options.rt.sunSouthTilt.tooltip: How many degrees south of the zenith the noon sun sits. 30 degrees reads like a temperate latitude; 0 passes straight overhead (tropical noon); larger tilts push midday shadows further.
caustica.options.rt.nameTags.tooltip: Render player and entity name tags in the world. Off hides every floating name above a head.
caustica.options.rt.blockOutline.tooltip: Draw the wireframe outline of the block you are aiming at over the ray-traced scene. Off hides it.
caustica.options.rt.waterWaveStrength.to: Multiplier on Animated Water's wave height and slope. 0.0x flattens the sea even with waves on; 1.0x is the tuned default; up to 4.0x turns a calm ocean into storm swell. Caustics stay in sync with the waves either way.
caustica.options.rt.waterWaveSpeed.toolt: Multiplier on Animated Water's animation clock. 0.0x freezes the sea in place; 1.0x is the default (physically based deep-water speeds); higher values push toward a time-lapse look. Changing it mid-session warps the wave phase once.
caustica.options.rt.waterWaveDetail.tool: How many wave-spectrum components Animated Water evaluates. The authored maximum is 7 (long 28 m swell down to ~1.6 m chop); lowering it drops the fine chop first and is the cheapest way to speed up large ocean views.
caustica.options.rt.parallaxQuality.tool: Sampling level of Parallax Occlusion Mapping: multiplies the per-hit height-field walk budget on top of the depth-derived base. Higher keeps fine relief intact at grazing angles on high-resolution packs (and costs more); lower saves GPU. Independent of POM Depth, which still sets how far the relief visually goes.
caustica.options.rt.cloudCoverage.toolti: Fraction of the sky the cloud deck covers in clear weather. Rain and thunderstorms drive the sky toward fully overcast on top of this; 0% leaves isolated wisps, 100% a nearly closed ceiling.
caustica.options.rt.cloudCoverage.classi: The classic deck is a single flat texture (like vanilla's clouds.png): its coverage is baked into the image, so this slider cannot change it. The volumetric deck renders the live coverage field with real depth — switch the style back to use the slider.
caustica.options.rt.fog.tooltip: Fog the light actually shines through: sun shafts, moon glow and torch cones are in-scattered per path segment and occluded by the same rays that shade the ground — so a cave stays dark and a cone stops at the wall that blocks it. Cost scales with samples per pixel, not with the number of lights. Off removes the medium entirely.
caustica.options.rt.fogDensity.tooltip: How thick the air is. One scattering coefficient drives both how fast distance darkens and how bright the light cones glow, so they can never disagree. 0% is no fog; 100% is a strong haze that swallows a 100-block view.
caustica.options.rt.fogDistance.tooltip: How far the fog integrates along a ray: closer than this, the haze dims and glows; beyond it, distance stops accumulating. Shorter keeps near-field shafts strong without burying the horizon.
caustica.options.rt.fogAnisotropy.toolti: Which way the fog scatters light. Higher concentrates the glow around whatever you look toward — opening up sun shafts and long torch beams — at the cost of dimmer side views; 0.00 glows evenly in every direction; negative values favour looking away from the light. Real dust and mist sit around 0.4 to 0.7.
caustica.options.rt.fogBiomeTint.tooltip: How much the fog's glow takes on the colour vanilla assigns to the air at your camera — the biome you stand in, greyed by rain, coloured by the dimension — the exact value vanilla's own fog fades to. 0% keeps every shaft the module's neutral cool white; 100% is vanilla's colour, so swamps green the sun beams and a thunderstorm greys everything out, no extra cost.
caustica.options.rt.fogHeightFalloff.too: Off keeps fog everywhere, mountain tops included. Any height turns it into valley mist: full density at and below world Y 90, decaying exponentially upward with this e-folding scale — 64 means a third of the density left 64 blocks above the fog line, and flying above it clears.
caustica.options.rt.risCandidates.toolti: Emitter light samples tested per shading point each frame before ReSTIR/RIS picks the best. Higher finds better lights in torch-dense scenes at extra cost; 0 disables point emitter sampling entirely (emissive blocks still glow when rays hit them directly).
caustica.options.rt.minFillRatio.tooltip: Drops emissive contributions that cover too little of a block from the light buffer. 0% keeps every light, however tiny; higher values skip sparse glow-lichen-style emitters and shrink the light list, at the risk of losing pinpoint lights.
caustica.options.rt.restirHistory.toolti: Temporal reuse amount: how much last frame's validated light reservoirs count for, in effective samples. MORE history damps flicker and crawling lights (at the price of ghosting when lights move); LESS tracks lighting changes faster but flickers more.
caustica.options.rt.restirSpatial.toolti: Spatial reuse: neighbouring reservoirs blended into each pixel per frame. More neighbours smooth reservoir noise and calm flicker (slower); 0 disables spatial reuse and keeps the purely temporal ReSTIR.
caustica.options.rt.restirMaxAge.tooltip: How many frames a light reservoir may live before history rejects and resamples it. Longer ages converge more (less flicker); shorter ages react faster to lighting changes.
caustica.options.rt.exposureKey.tooltip: The scene brightness level auto exposure aims to land on middle grey. 0.18 is the photographic standard; lower values darken the whole exposure curve, higher ones brighten it.
caustica.options.rt.exposureMinEv.toolti: Dark limit for auto exposure: it never compensates below this, keeping night scenes night. If crossed with Max EV the two swap roles.
caustica.options.rt.exposureMaxEv.toolti: Bright limit for auto exposure: it never compensates above this, keeping the sun from blowing out the image. If crossed with Min EV the two swap roles.
caustica.options.rt.adaptUp.tooltip: How fast auto exposure brightens when the scene darkens (the eye-adjusting-to-a-cave speed). Lower is more cinematic; higher reacts faster but can pump.
caustica.options.rt.adaptDown.tooltip: How fast auto exposure darkens when the scene gets brighter. Faster downward than upward adaptation keeps highlights under control when you look toward the sun.
caustica.options.rt.reflexBoost.tooltip: Lets Reflex keep the GPU clocks up, shaving a little extra latency when the game is GPU-bound. Minor extra power draw; off by default.
caustica.options.rt.reflexMinInterval.to: Reflex-side framerate cap in microseconds per frame (for example 16667 us = 60 fps). 0 disables the cap and lets Reflex only pace submission.
caustica.options.rt.asyncDispatch.toolti: Max terrain sections queued to the background meshers per streaming pass. Higher rebuilds faster after teleports and at world load; lower keeps render-thread work flatter on weak CPUs.
caustica.options.rt.resultsPerPass.toolt: Max built terrain sections the render thread publishes per streaming pass. Higher fills the BLAS/OMM pipelines faster after big camera cuts; lower spreads out the render-thread spike.
caustica.options.rt.maxInflight.tooltip: How many terrain sections may be mid-rebuild at once (snapshot -> worker mesh -> GPU build). Bounds queue depth and pinned snapshot memory when flying fast; raise it if terrain visibly trails behind you.
caustica.options.rt.blasCompaction.toolt: Compact terrain acceleration structures after building them: roughly halves BLAS memory at a slightly longer build time. The terrain fully rebuilds when you change this, so no section is left in the old state.
caustica.options.rt.ommSubdivision.toolt: Micro-triangle subdivision level for opacity micromaps (0 = coarser/cheaper, up to 6 = tightest cutout masks). Higher levels fit leaf and grass silhouettes more precisely. The terrain fully rebuilds when you change this.
caustica.options.rt.frameStats.tooltip: Log per-frame RT timings and hitch reports to the console (per render-stage breakdowns). Off keeps the log quiet.
caustica.options.rt.ommStats.tooltip: Log opacity-micromap build statistics to the console. Debug information only.
caustica.options.rt.lightStats.tooltip: Log direct-light buffer statistics (emitter counts, grid occupancy) to the console. Debug information only.
caustica.options.rt.lightDump.tooltip: Dump the emitter lights around the player to the console whenever the light grid updates. Heavy spam: enable only while debugging a missing light.
caustica.options.rt.lightDumpRadius.tool: Radius in blocks around the camera for the Light Dump emitter listing.
caustica.options.rt.fgEngine.tooltip: Which frame-generation engine synthesizes the intermediate frames. Caustica Native interpolates with the path tracer's exact motion vectors on any GPU and supports up to 4x multipliers; AMD FSR 3.1 is the signed AMD runtime, a reference alternative fixed at 2x.
